standard: RFC 9449 §10.1, taken in by FAPI 2.0 §5.3.2.1 item 12
text: An AS accepts the DPoP key from the PAR request's DPoP header alone
behaviour: `dpop_jkt` is required in the signed JAR. A DPoP header on PAR must match it; a header alone is refused
why: With the header alone, a compromised Front reposts the RP's JAR with its own key's header, binds T to the attacker's key, and gets both the victim's token and the key it is bound to (Tamarin `PAR_DPOP_HEADER_ONLY`)

text: Members of a claims request that are not understood MUST be ignored
behaviour: The direct members of `id_token` and `userinfo` written as null are read as `{}` (the same meaning). Any other null in `claims` is refused at /login/start with 400 `invalid_request_object`
why: The statement T the person approves is signed whole, and the signer writes no null (OIDC Core §13.3). A part of the request that cannot be signed as given is refused before the person is asked, never silently dropped from what they approve

text: `dpop_jkt` is an optional authorization request parameter; FAPI does not require the client to send it
why: When the Front relays the token request, binding the authorization to the RP's DPoP key in the signed request is what keeps a compromised Front from redeeming the code under its own key (claim 1)

text: A confidential client's refresh token need not be bound to the DPoP key; FAPI names rotating the key without losing the grant as a benefit
behaviour: A confidential client's refresh family is bound to the authorization's DPoP key; a refresh under another key is refused
why: A family not bound to the key can be refreshed by whoever holds the token, including a compromised Front that saw it (claim 2)

behaviour: `authorization_details` is refused at PAR and on every grant at the token endpoint
why: Per-operation authorization belongs to the RS and 4s-intent, not the IdP (V6); accepting it would make the IdP decide operations

text: The Security Profile accepts an authorization request without a signed request object
behaviour: Every authorization request is a signed JAR (PAR in a FAPI configuration, F4)
why: Without a signed request, a compromised Front rewrites the request the person approves (claim 1's code-grant hole). Applies only if the Security Profile plan is run

standard: RFC 6749 §4.1.2; OAuth 2.0 Multiple Response Type Encoding Practices §2.1; RFC 9207; FAPI 2.0 Security Profile
text: An AS may return the authorization response in the redirect URI's query, made safe by `iss` (RFC 9207); the client may leave `response_mode` out
behaviour: A JAR must carry `response_mode=form_post`; the response is a POST to the redirect URI, never its query
why: Against login CSRF: the RP's callback takes the response by `form_post` alone and checks that its `Origin` is exactly the login screen's, its `state` cookie `SameSite=None; Secure`, so a response another site sends the victim's browser is refused

text: A request object may leave `jti` out
behaviour: A JAR without `jti` is refused; one JAR starts one login, held by its client and `jti` until its expiry and the clock skew
why: The Core uses one JAR, and its `request_uri`, for one statement T alone, which needs the JAR named

text: A client should send `typ` `oauth-authz-req+jwt` (FAPI 2.0 Message Signing); the AS need not require it
behaviour: A JAR without `typ` `oauth-authz-req+jwt` is refused; the type is compared as a media type, without case
why: Explicit typing keeps a JWT made for another purpose with the same client key from being passed off as a request object

text: An AS refuses a request object whose `exp` is more than 60 minutes after its `nbf`
behaviour: PAR refuses a JAR whose `exp` is further than its own `jar-max-lifetime` (90 seconds by default) from the time it takes it; the login's start checks it again against `authorize`'s
why: A short `exp` and the Core's own cap keep long-lived JARs from piling up reservations
